pages.title: Slide 2
pages.text:
Why is this Important?
• We’ve spent time thinking about the various building blocks which make
  up our cells
• This included proteins – one of the most important building blocks we
  have
• Proteins are used for lots of things in our cells, tissues, and organs –
  including helping in the manufacture of other building blocks that we’ve
  learned about
• But like any good structure, there’s a blueprint for these proteins – that’s
  our DNA and the genes within it!
• So, it’s important for us to know about these so we can fully understand
  how proteins are “coded” or “blueprinted”!
• As always, we need to know what happens here when things are right, so
  that we can appreciate what happens when things go wrong!

The Structure of DNA, Genes, and Genomes

Part 1. A Basic Introduction to DNA

media.webLabel: Open slide 3 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 4
pages.jumpLabel: So, What is DNA, and What are Genes?
pages.text:
So, What is DNA, and What are Genes?
• In short, the DNA, and the genes located within it are the blueprint
  of life
• We can think of this in a similar way to computer code…
• …but a code which both codes for the building of the hardware, as
  well as telling that hardware how to function!
• We refer to this as our genetic code
• These codes provide the instructions which allow organisms to
  function – this often involves the onward production of other
  materials that we need to survive – not just proteins!
• We can install this code on future devices – our children - allowing
  them to function correctly, and to obtain our traits and characteristics!

media.webLabel: Open slide 4 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 5
pages.text:
Where do we find DNA?
• This is hopefully something that you remember!
• Most of the time, we’ll find the DNA in the nucleus of
  our cells
• The nucleus acts as
  safe storage for our
  genetic material, and the
  control centre for the
  cell’s function – we’ll see
  lots of processes taking
  place here!

media.webLabel: Open slide 5 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

We’ll talk about how our bodies
  ”run” this software, and how this
 software is passed from device to
 device, in later lectures – for now,
     we want to focus on the key
    aspects of what our DNA and
genes are - we have to understand

Part 2. DNA Structure
– The Basics

media.webLabel: Open slide 7 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 8
pages.text:
DNA Building Blocks – The Nucleotide
• DNA = DeoxyriboNucleic Acid
• This name relates to the nature of the material which DNA is
  made from – the nucleotides…
• …and also where it’s found – in the nucleus!
• The nucleotides have three key components:
   • A deoxyribose pentose sugar
   • A phosphate group – which gives the DNA its overall acidic
     nature
   • A nitrogen-containing (nitrogenous) base
• We’ll see differences in those bases in each of the different
  nucleotides!

practice.title: Reading a nucleotide drawing
practice.prompt: Two students label the same DNA nucleotide. One labels an entire nucleotide as a base. The other circles just the ring structure containing nitrogen. Which label would you keep, and what two components would you add to show the complete building block?
practice.answer: Keep the label on the nitrogen-containing ring structure for the base. A complete DNA nucleotide also includes deoxyribose and a phosphate group.

pages.title: Slide 11
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Across or along a strand?
pages.text:
Bonding in DNA

• When it comes to DNA, there are a couple of key bonds
  that we need to know about and remember!
• The phosphodiester bond is what holds nucleotides
  together to form the backbone of single-stranded DNA
• Hydrogen bonds hold the strands of DNA together in
  double-stranded DNA, through the interaction between
  the bases in each of the strands – this is responsible for
  DNA’s double-helix structure!

media.webLabel: Open slide 11 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Across or along a strand?
practice.prompt: A diagram has two callouts. One points between paired bases on opposite strands. The other points between neighbouring nucleotides along one strand. What bond belongs at each callout, and what feature of the drawing settles the choice?
practice.answer: The across-strand interaction is hydrogen bonding between bases. Along one backbone, phosphodiester bonds join neighbouring nucleotides. The location of each callout is the evidence.

pages.title: Slide 13
pages.text:
Joining the Strands
• At this point, we know about the basic structure of DNA,
  what holds this together, and how nucleotides are
  connected into single strands with a phosphate backbone
• In its resting state, a DNA molecule usually exists as a
  double helix, made up of two single nucleotide strands that
  run in opposite directions
• Quick note: When we talk about a “DNA molecule” in
  general, we usually mean this double-stranded form - if
  we want to describe one half of it, we’ll say “a single strand
  of DNA”
• This is where those hydrogen bonds come in!
• When it comes to the formation of these helices, there are
  some rules that we need to be aware of!

media.webLabel: Open slide 13 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 14
pages.text:
Joining the Strands – The Rules
• As the single strands come together to form
  the DNA molecule, the rules of
  complementary base pairing come into
  play
• What this means is that:
   • An adenine (A) in one strand can only
     bind to a thymine (T) in the other
   • A cytosine (C) in one strand can only
     bind to a guanine (G) in the other
• The bonding between these bases holds the
  strands together in an antiparallel
  formation – this means that the two strands
  of DNA run in opposite directions to one
  another

media.webLabel: Open slide 14 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 15
pages.text:
The Groovy Double Helix
• It’s important to remember that as the bases
  come together to form the double helix, that they
  aren’t all the same size and shape
• So, they don’t form a perfect coil
• This means that the strands aren’t a constant
  distance from one another, which can squash
  and stretch the helix
• This gives us the minor and major grooves
• The wider major groove provides attachment
  points for things to bind to the DNA – this is
  useful for a range of processes

media.webLabel: Open slide 15 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 16
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Two labels for one drawing
pages.text:
More Coiling – Fitting in all our DNA
• The coiling of DNA molecules into a double helix helps to make it more
  compact – this is useful, as there’s not enough space to store linear
  chains of DNA within the nucleus of our cells
• But, at this point, each molecule is still about two metres in length!
• So, we need more coiling!
• The next level of coiling involves the wrapping of DNA strands around
  histone proteins – this gives us nucleosomes, when then go on to
  form a complex called chromatin, which is a thick fibre made of these
  nucleosome loops
• This fibre is then bunched up into even more loops, which stick to a
  protein scaffold, allowing the DNA to compress itself even more
• Finally, these protein scaffolds fold to give us our chromosomes!

media.webLabel: Open slide 16 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Two labels for one drawing
practice.prompt: A sketch shows DNA wrapped around a group of proteins. One arrow points to a protein and a bracket surrounds the DNA plus the proteins. How would you label the arrow and the bracket differently?
practice.answer: The arrow points to a histone. The bracket encloses a nucleosome, which includes the histones and the DNA wrapped around them.

More Coiling

media.webLabel: Open slide 17 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 18
pages.text:
The Chromosome – Ultimate DNA
Coiling

• Each chromosome contains a SINGLE molecule of
  double-stranded DNA, which is supercoiled to a level
  which allows it to fit into the nucleus!
• Not all of our DNA is held in a single chromosome
• We have 46 different ones (in 23 pairs), each of which
  contain different DNA chains, and thus different genes!
• Great! But - what are genes?

media.webLabel: Open slide 18 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 19
pages.jumpLabel: The Structure of DNA, Genes, and Genomes
pages.text:
The Structure of DNA, Genes, and Genomes

Part 3. What are Genes?

media.webLabel: Open slide 19 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 20
pages.jumpLabel: Genes are the DNA’s Computer Code
pages.text:
Genes are the DNA’s Computer Code
• Up until now, we’ve thought simply about DNA as being a collection of nucleotide
  bases joined together in chains which are then coiled around one another
• That’s great, but – so what?!
• Within the single chains of DNA which make up the double-strand, we’ll find
  sections which actually code for something – a particular protein
• That code can be read by other hardware in the cell, which uses it as a blueprint
  to make those proteins
• Those sections of DNA are genes – we have around 20,000 of them!
• These are the blocks of code that allows us to be built and maintained
• Genes are hereditary – they’re transferred from parent to child…
• …providing the child with the code it needs to function as a human more
  generally, but also with inherited characteristics – things like eye colour and
  height!

media.webLabel: Open slide 20 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 21
pages.jumpLabel: Practice · Evaluating a claim about DNA
pages.text:
All DNA is Important
• Knowing what a gene is, you might then assume that all the other DNA
  we have in our chromosomes which aren’t genes isn’t of any use
• You wouldn’t be alone here - this non-gene DNA used to be referred to
  as “junk DNA”
• But, you’d be VERY wrong!
• Those parts of the DNA carry out a range of roles:
   • Some help to control which genes are turned on and when
   • Some help to control how much a gene is turned on or off
   • Some are structural – they’ll help the chromosome to form, protect
     it from degradation, and help it to keep its shape
   • …and that’s just the stuff that we know about!

media.webLabel: Open slide 21 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

practice.title: Evaluating a claim about DNA
practice.prompt: A colleague suggests leaving every region outside protein-coding genes off a diagram because those regions have no function. Give one reason the proposed diagram could mislead a reader.
practice.answer: Some non-coding regions help control when or how much a gene is expressed. Others contribute to chromosome structure or protection. Either example shows why removing them all loses biological information.

pages.title: Slide 22
pages.text:
Gene Structure
• As you’d expect, these blocks of genetic code are complicated – they have
  multiple parts!
• The promoter is the site where a specialised protein binds to trigger the
  reading of the code – we’ll talk more about that later!
• The exons are the parts of the gene which provide the actual code for the
  protein in question
• The introns are parts of the gene which don’t code for proteins, and are
  removed as the code is processed – they play roles in the regulation of gene
  expression and other things!

pages.title: Slide 24
pages.jumpLabel: Gene Detail – Back to the DNA Code
pages.text:
Gene Detail – Back to the DNA Code
• At this point then, we know what genes are, and how they’re
  structured
• It’s important not to forget that they’re still sequences of As, Ts, Cs,
  and Gs lined up in a particular sequence within a single strand of a
  DNA molecule
• It is that sequence of As, Ts, Cs, and Gs which makes the code work
  – and this is very specific and complex!
• A change in a single nucleotide in a sequence can lead to the
  eventual production of a protein which won’t have the structure
  and/or function necessary – this can lead to disease!
• This is made even more impressive when we consider the size of
  genes – our biggest has 79 exons and is 2.3 million bases long!

media.webLabel: Open slide 24 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 25
pages.text:
Gene Detail – The Codon
• As we dig deeper into the DNA code within each gene, we
  realise that nucleotides work together to allow the code to work
• Within the gene’s DNA code, groups of three nucleotides
  team up to form codons
• During the transcription of this code, and its translation into a
  protein, those codons are what eventually specify which
  amino acid is placed in which part of the protein chain
  coded by a gene
• As we already know, the location of an amino acid within a
  protein is crucial to its function – and this starts with these
  codons being correct in the first place!

media.webLabel: Open slide 25 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 26
pages.jumpLabel: We’ll discuss this in lots more detail when we’re
pages.text:
We’ll discuss this in lots more detail when we’re
  considering transcription and translation!

For now, it’s important for you to know what genes
are, and where they lie within our genetic material
 – not every bit of our DNA ends up coding for a
                      protein!

media.webLabel: Open slide 26 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 27
pages.jumpLabel: The Structure of DNA, Genes, and Genomes
pages.text:
The Structure of DNA, Genes, and Genomes

Part 4. The Genome

media.webLabel: Open slide 27 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 28
pages.text:
What is the Genome?

• So far, as we’ve been talking about our genes we’ve been
  considering small chunks of our DNA – individual genes
• The genome is our DNA on a larger scale
• It is the entire set of DNA instructions found in a cell
• It’s all of the contents of our chromosomes
• Being able to picture and understand the genome would allow us to
  unlock the entire blueprint for how we work
• This is useful for understanding health, and illness!
• But, it’s VERY complicated – the genome sequence is literally a full
  list of all of those As, Ts, Cs, and Gs which are in our chromosomes!

media.webLabel: Open slide 28 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 29
pages.jumpLabel: The Human Genome – Coding vs Non-
pages.text:
The Human Genome – Coding vs Non-
Coding
• We already know that some of our DNA doesn’t code for anything…
• …but it’s also not “junk”!
• The Human Genome Project sought to, amongst other things, work
  out how much of our genome coded for proteins
• In early 2022, this work was completed, providing a picture of the
  three billion base pairs we possess!
• All of this has told us that less than 1% of our DNA codes for
  proteins!
• This demonstrates both the size, and importance of those non-
  coding regions, which do lots of things to keep us functioning
  correctly

media.webLabel: Open slide 29 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 30
pages.text:
Genomes – Organism Differences
• Earlier in this module, we briefly compared eukaryotic organisms
  (including us!) to prokaryotic ones
• One of the key differences in these organisms relates to their genetic
  material
• Both groups possess DNA, but this appears differently in both!
• For example:
   • Prokaryotic DNA is smaller in size, arranged in circular structures, and
     located in the cytoplasm
   • Prokaryotic DNA doesn’t have introns, and genes are held much more
     closely together
   • The arrangement of material within the genome is much less complex
     generally, including in relation to where the duplication of DNA starts

media.webLabel: Open slide 30 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 31
pages.text:
Organism Differences – Useful for
Drug Development!
• One key difference between prokaryotes and eukaryotes is that
  plasmids exist in prokaryotes
• These plasmids are circular pieces of DNA which are less complex,
  and which can be easily modified
• This allows us to easily “swap out” some of the content of the
  plasmid, changing its blueprint, and giving it instructions for a
  particular protein
• This means that we can add a human gene into one of those
  plasmids with some processing, allowing bacteria to produce that
  protein for us – genetic recombination!

media.webLabel: Open slide 31 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 32
pages.text:
The diagram illustrates a general use of plasmids as carriers of a gene of interest; it links a human gene, a circular plasmid and a bacterial cell.

Organism Differences – Useful for

media.webLabel: Open slide 32 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 33
pages.text:
Different Organisms – Different
Complexities

• When comparing genomes, it’s clear to see
  that there is a significant range in genome
  size and complexity
• This is true across eukaryotes
• Don’t assume that we’re the most complex
  organism out there in terms of genetics!
• We have three billion base pairs, but what
  about Paris japonica?

               149 billion!

media.webLabel: Open slide 33 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 34
pages.text:
To Sum Up…
• We should now understand the structure of the blueprint for our protein
  building blocks…
• …what the key parts of a nucleotide are, and the differences between the
  four nucleotides which make up our DNA
• We also know how these bases come together to form single DNA strands,
  then double-stranded double helix DNA molecules, and ultimately,
  chromosomes – after a lot of coiling!
• We should also now know what a gene is, what these consist of, and how
  they can be very complicated – this complexity translates directly into the
  manufacture of complicated proteins which do complicated jobs!
• All of this information provides us with information about our full blueprint –
  our genome – as we learn to understand this more, we’ll learn more about
  how we work, and how we can fix ourselves if our genes go wrong!

media.webLabel: Open slide 34 in Dr Dan Corbett’s original PDF

pages.title: Slide 35
pages.text:
Next Time…

• We’ll think about how our genetic blueprint goes from
  DNA code to protein
• This will start with the process of transcription, which
  converts our DNA into a slightly different code…
• …which is then translated into a protein, which can go
  on to carry out its function in the body
• All of this will allow us to think about the entire process
  of how we can get a protein from a gene, which is the
  basis of how we work!
